items.title: ISRO — Evolution, Organisation & Launch Vehicles
items.body:
## In one line
How India's space agency grew from a 1962 committee into ISRO, and the family of rockets it uses to reach orbit.

## The story
India's space effort began as **INCOSPAR** (Indian National Committee for Space Research) in **1962**, set up by **Vikram Sarabhai** — the "father of the Indian space programme". It was reorganised into the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on 15 August 1969**. In **1972** the government created the **Department of Space (DoS)** and the Space Commission, and ISRO has worked under DoS ever since. After Sarabhai, leaders like **Satish Dhawan** built the institutions, followed by chairmen such as U R Rao, Kasturirangan, K. Sivan and S. Somanath.

To put satellites in space you need **launch vehicles** (rockets). India built a ladder of them, each for a different job:
- **PSLV** — the reliable **"workhorse"** that reaches Low Earth Orbit and even flung Chandrayaan-1 and Mangalyaan on their way.
- **GSLV** — carries heavy communication satellites to high geostationary orbit, using an indigenous **cryogenic** (super-cold fuel) upper stage.
- **LVM3 (GSLV Mk-III)** — the **heaviest operational** rocket; it launched Chandrayaan-3 and will carry Gaganyaan.
- **SSLV** — a small rocket for small satellites (~500 kg), built for quick "launch-on-demand".
- **NGLV** — a next-generation heavy-lift rocket, still under development.

## Why it matters
Examiners love matching each rocket to its role and payload, and the INCOSPAR→ISRO→DoS timeline. These are near-certain Paper-II facts.

## Picture it

| Vehicle | Job |
|---|---|
| PSLV | Workhorse — LEO/SSO; Chandrayaan-1, MOM |
| GSLV | Heavy comsats to geostationary orbit |
| LVM3 (Mk-III) | Heaviest; Chandrayaan-3, Gaganyaan |
| SSLV | Small sats (~500 kg) to LEO |

## Terms explained
- **LEO** — Low Earth Orbit, a few hundred km up.
- **Geostationary orbit** — ~36,000 km up, where a satellite seems to hover over one spot.
- **Cryogenic stage** — a rocket stage burning super-cold liquid fuel (very high thrust).
- **Payload** — the satellite or cargo the rocket carries.

## Don't confuse
**PSLV** is the light-to-medium workhorse; **LVM3** is the heavy-lifter. Heavy Moon/crew missions need LVM3, not PSLV.

## Remember it
"**P for Performer, L for Lifter**" — PSLV the dependable performer, LVM3 the heavy lifter.

## TL;DR
- INCOSPAR (1962, Sarabhai) → ISRO (15 Aug 1969) → Department of Space (1972).
- PSLV = workhorse (Chandrayaan-1, MOM); LVM3 = heaviest (Chandrayaan-3).
- GSLV = comsats (cryogenic stage); SSLV = small sats (~500 kg); NGLV in development.
- Satellite families: INSAT/GSAT (comms), IRS (remote sensing), NavIC (navigation).
keyPoints: INCOSPAR (1962) under Vikram Sarabhai became ISRO on 15 August 1969; Department of Space created 1972.
PSLV is ISRO's workhorse (Chandrayaan-1, MOM); LVM3/GSLV Mk-III is the heaviest operational launcher.
SSLV serves small satellites (~500 kg) to LEO; NGLV is the next-gen heavy-lift vehicle under development.
Satellite families: INSAT/GSAT (communication), IRS (remote sensing), NavIC (navigation).
Applications include tele-education, telemedicine, weather, disaster warning and cartography.

items.title: Flagship Missions — Chandrayaan, Aditya, Gaganyaan, SpaDeX, NISAR
items.body:
## In one line
India's recent headline space missions — a Moon landing, a Sun observatory, human spaceflight prep, in-space docking and an Earth-radar satellite — and what comes next.

## The story
A run of landmark missions has made India a serious space power:
- **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, MOM)** — India's **Mars orbiter**, launched on PSLV in November 2013 and in Mars orbit from September 2014; India reached Mars on its first attempt.
- **Chandrayaan-3 (23 August 2023)** — the first ever soft landing near the **lunar south pole** (the Moon's south polar region), making India the **4th nation** to soft-land on the Moon. Lander **Vikram**, rover **Pragyan**, landing site named **Shiv Shakti Point**.
- **Aditya-L1** — India's first solar mission; launched 2 Sep 2023 and parked in a **halo orbit around the Sun-Earth point L1** (~1.5 million km away) on **6 Jan 2024**, giving an unbroken view of the Sun. Main payload: VELC.
- **Gaganyaan** — India's human spaceflight programme: it aims to send Indian astronauts (three crew) to about 400 km in Low Earth Orbit aboard an **indigenous crew module** on the **human-rated LVM3**. The **TV-D1 test (Oct 2023)** proved the crew-escape system through an in-flight abort; **four IAF pilots** were named astronaut-designates in Feb 2024 (one, Shubhanshu Shukla, flew to the ISS on Axiom-4 in 2025). Uncrewed test flights are planned first; the crewed flight is targeted around 2026-27.
- **SpaDeX** — launched on PSLV-C60 (30 Dec 2024); **docking of two satellites achieved on 16 Jan 2025**, making India the **4th nation** to dock in space — a must-have skill for a space station and sample-return.
- **NISAR (30 July 2025)** — a joint **ISRO-NASA** Earth-observation satellite, the first with **dual-frequency (L-band + S-band) radar**, watching land/ice movement, ecosystems and hazards.

Looking ahead: **Chandrayaan-4** (lunar sample return, ~2028), **Shukrayaan** (Venus orbiter), the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035**, and an **Indian on the Moon by 2040**.

## Why it matters
These missions, with exact dates and "which number nation" facts, are the single most-asked current-affairs cluster in space. Dates and firsts must be precise.

## Picture it

| Mission | Date | Claim to fame |
|---|---|---|
| Chandrayaan-3 | 23 Aug 2023 | First south-pole soft landing |
| Aditya-L1 | L1 on 6 Jan 2024 | First solar mission |
| SpaDeX | docked 16 Jan 2025 | 4th nation to dock |
| NISAR | 30 Jul 2025 | Dual-band radar (ISRO-NASA) |

| Mission | Objective |
|---|---|
| Mangalyaan (MOM) | Mars orbiter |
| Chandrayaan-4 | Lunar sample return |
| Shukrayaan | Venus orbiter |
| NavIC (IRNSS) | Regional navigation (India + ~1,500 km) |

## Terms explained
- **Lagrange point L1** — a balance point between Sun and Earth where a satellite can sit using little fuel.
- **Docking** — joining two spacecraft together in orbit.
- **SAR** — Synthetic Aperture Radar, which images the ground day or night, through clouds.
- **Human-rated** — a rocket certified safe to carry people.

## Don't confuse
**Aditya-L1 does not land on or touch the Sun** — it orbits the L1 balance point to observe the Sun from a safe 1.5 million km.

## Remember it
Order of firsts "**C-A-G-S-N**": Chandrayaan-3 → Aditya → Gaganyaan test → SpaDeX → NISAR.

## TL;DR
- Chandrayaan-3 (23 Aug 2023): first south-pole landing; Vikram/Pragyan/Shiv Shakti Point.
- Aditya-L1 reached halo orbit around L1 on 6 Jan 2024.
- Gaganyaan: 3 crew on human-rated LVM3; TV-D1 tested escape; 4 pilots named 2024.
- SpaDeX: first Indian in-space docking, 16 Jan 2025 (4th nation).
- NISAR (Jul 2025): ISRO-NASA dual-band radar. Future: Chandrayaan-4 (~2028), BAS 2035, Moon 2040.
keyPoints: Chandrayaan-3 (23 Aug 2023): first south-pole soft landing; lander Vikram, rover Pragyan, site Shiv Shakti Point.
Aditya-L1 reached a halo orbit around Sun-Earth L1 on 6 Jan 2024 — India's first solar mission.
Gaganyaan: 3 crew to LEO on human-rated LVM3; TV-D1 (2023) tested crew escape; crew named Feb 2024.
SpaDeX achieved India's first in-space docking on 16 Jan 2025 — the 4th nation to do so.
NISAR (Jul 2025) is the ISRO-NASA dual-frequency (L & S band) SAR Earth-observation satellite.
Vision: Chandrayaan-4 sample return (~2028), Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, Indian on Moon by 2040.
items.mnemonic: Order of recent firsts: 'C-A-G-S-N' = Chandrayaan-3 → Aditya → Gaganyaan test → SpaDeX → NISAR.

items.title: NavIC, Private Space & Sriharikota (AP)
items.body:
## In one line
India's own regional GPS (NavIC), the opening of space to private companies, and the Andhra Pradesh spaceport that launches it all.

## The story
**NavIC (IRNSS)** is India's **own regional navigation system** — like GPS, but covering only **India and about 1,500 km around it** (it can be extended). It is built and run by **ISRO** with a constellation designed around **7 satellites** (3 in geostationary and 4 in geosynchronous orbits). It gives a civilian **Standard Positioning Service** and a secure **Restricted Service**; newer satellites add an **L1 signal** so ordinary smartphones can use NavIC.

Space is no longer government-only. **IN-SPACe** is the single-window body that **authorises and promotes** private space activity, while **NSIL (New Space India Limited)** is ISRO's commercial arm that sells launches and satellites. Start-ups have arrived: **Skyroot** flew **Vikram-S**, India's first private rocket, in 2022, and **Agnikul** built the **Agnibaan** with a 3D-printed engine.

All of this lifts off from **Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh**, home of **SDSC-SHAR** — India's primary **spaceport** on the Bay of Bengal, launching PSLV, GSLV and LVM3. Its **near-equatorial, east-coast** location lets rockets launch **eastward over the sea** (safe and fuel-efficient, using Earth's spin). It is named after **Satish Dhawan**. A **second spaceport** at Kulasekarapattinam (Tamil Nadu) is being built for the small SSLV, but SHAR remains AP's strategic space asset.

## Why it matters
NavIC-vs-GPS, the IN-SPACe/NSIL reforms, and Sriharikota's location advantage are repeat exam points — especially the AP angle.

## Picture it

| System | Coverage | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| GPS / GLONASS / Galileo / BeiDou | Global | USA / Russia / EU / China |
| NavIC (IRNSS) | India + ~1,500 km | India (ISRO) |

## Terms explained
- **Constellation** — a group of satellites working together.
- **Geostationary / geosynchronous** — high orbits where a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation.
- **Spaceport** — the launch base for rockets.
- **IN-SPACe** — the regulator-promoter for private space; **NSIL** — ISRO's commercial company.

## Don't confuse
**NavIC is regional, not global.** It is India's own system — not GPS, and not a joint venture with Galileo.

## Remember it
"**NavIC = Navigation with Indian Constellation, near home only**" — regional, Indian-built.

## TL;DR
- NavIC/IRNSS = regional navigation (7-satellite design) covering India + ~1,500 km; newer sats add L1 for phones.
- IN-SPACe authorises/promotes private space; NSIL is ISRO's commercial arm.
- Skyroot's Vikram-S (2022) = India's first private rocket; Agnikul builds Agnibaan.
- SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota (AP) = India's primary spaceport; east-coast location aids eastward launches.
keyPoints: NavIC/IRNSS is a regional system (7-satellite constellation) covering India + ~1,500 km, unlike global GPS; newer satellites add the L1 civilian signal.
IN-SPACe authorises/promotes private space; NSIL is ISRO's commercial arm.
Skyroot's Vikram-S (2022) was India's first private rocket; Agnikul builds the Agnibaan with a 3D-printed engine.
SDSC-SHAR at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh is India's primary spaceport for PSLV/GSLV/LVM3.
Sriharikota's near-equatorial east-coast location enables efficient, safe eastward launches.

items.title: DRDO & the Missile Arsenal (IGMDP)
items.body:
## In one line
India's defence research body and the family of missiles it built — from short-range Prithvi to the intercontinental Agni — plus its newest strategic capabilities.

## The story
The **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)**, formed in **1958**, is India's main defence-R&D body, with 50+ laboratories. In **1983** it launched the **Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP)** under **A.P.J. Abdul Kalam** to build a home-grown missile arsenal.

Each missile has a distinct job:
- **Prithvi** — short-range surface-to-surface ballistic missile.
- **Agni** — the long-range ballistic family; **Agni-V** (5,000+ km) tested **MIRV — Multiple Independently-targetable Re-entry Vehicle** technology (many warheads from one missile) for the first time under **Mission Divyastra (March 2024)**.
- **Akash** — medium-range surface-to-air (shoots down aircraft).
- **Astra** — beyond-visual-range air-to-air (fired from fighter jets).
- **Nag** — anti-tank guided missile.
- **BrahMos** — Indo-Russian **supersonic cruise** missile (~Mach 2.8), launchable from land, sea, submarine and air.

Beyond the IGMDP, India has grown **strategic** muscle: **Mission Shakti (2019)** used an anti-satellite (ASAT) missile to intercept a live satellite in low Earth orbit, making India the 4th such nation after the USA, Russia and China; a two-tier **Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD)** shield; **hypersonic** work (the HSTDV demonstrator); and **K-series submarine-launched missiles** (K-15, K-4) that complete the **nuclear triad** (the ability to fire nuclear weapons from land, air and sea).

## Why it matters
Matching missiles to their category, the IGMDP-Kalam link, and the Agni-V MIRV/Mission Shakti milestones are classic Paper-II and Mains facts.

## Picture it

| Missile | Category |
|---|---|
| Prithvi | Short-range surface-to-surface ballistic |
| Agni | Ballistic (Agni-V 5,000+ km, MIRV) |
| Akash | Surface-to-air |
| Astra | Air-to-air (beyond visual range) |
| Nag | Anti-tank |
| BrahMos | Supersonic cruise (Indo-Russian) |

## Terms explained
- **Ballistic missile** — follows a high arcing path, mostly unpowered after launch.
- **Cruise missile** — flies low and powered like an aircraft (e.g. BrahMos).
- **MIRV** — one missile carrying several warheads aimed at different targets.
- **ASAT** — anti-satellite weapon.
- **Nuclear triad** — nuclear strike from land, air and sea.

## Don't confuse
**Agni = ballistic** (arcing, long-range); **BrahMos = cruise** (low, fast, powered). They are different missile types.

## Remember it
IGMDP missiles "**PATNA**" = Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Nag, Akash.

## TL;DR
- DRDO (1958) runs the IGMDP (1983), spearheaded by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
- IGMDP: Prithvi (SS ballistic), Agni (ballistic), Akash (SAM), Trishul (SAM), Nag (anti-tank).
- Agni-V (5,000+ km) tested MIRV under Mission Divyastra (March 2024).
- BrahMos = Indo-Russian supersonic cruise missile (~Mach 2.8).
- Mission Shakti (2019) = ASAT; plus two-tier BMD, HSTDV hypersonics, K-series SLBMs (triad).
keyPoints: DRDO (formed 1958) runs the IGMDP (1983), spearheaded by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
IGMDP missiles: Prithvi (SS ballistic), Agni (ballistic), Akash (SAM), Trishul (SAM), Nag (anti-tank).
Agni-V (5,000+ km) tested MIRV under Mission Divyastra (March 2024).
BrahMos is an Indo-Russian supersonic cruise missile (~Mach 2.8), land/sea/sub/air-launched.
Mission Shakti (2019) demonstrated ASAT; DRDO also pursues two-tier BMD and HSTDV hypersonics.
items.mnemonic: IGMDP missiles = 'PATNA' → Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Nag, Akash.

items.title: Defence Indigenisation & Operation Sindoor (2025)
items.body:
## In one line
India's drive to design and build its own weapons (Atmanirbhar Bharat), and the 2025 operation that tested its integrated air defence.

## The story
**Self-reliance in defence** (Atmanirbhar Bharat) means designing and making weapons at home instead of importing them. India now fields **indigenous platforms**: **Tejas** (Light Combat Aircraft, built by HAL), the **Arjun** main battle tank, Dhruv/Prachand helicopters, and the home-built aircraft carrier **INS Vikrant**.

The push is backed by **policy levers**: the **Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020**, which prefers buying from Indian makers ("**Buy (Indian-IDDM)**" — Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured); **iDEX**, which funds defence start-ups and small firms; **positive indigenisation lists** that ban importing specified items; and rising defence exports.

**Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025)** was a military operation launching **precision strikes on cross-border terror infrastructure** after the Pahalgam attack (April 2025). It showcased a **layered, integrated air defence**: the Russian-origin **S-400 system (in Indian service as 'Sudarshan Chakra')**, the indigenous **Akash** surface-to-air missile, and counter-drone systems working together in a networked command. The lesson: strengthen **indigenous air defence, drones and long-range precision munitions** (including BrahMos) — feeding the Atmanirbhar Bharat drive.

## Why it matters
Indigenisation policy (DAP 2020, iDEX) and the Operation Sindoor air-defence story are high-value for both Paper-II and Mains (strategic autonomy).

## Picture it

| Lever | What it does |
|---|---|
| DAP 2020 | Prefers 'Buy (Indian-IDDM)' |
| iDEX | Funds defence start-ups/MSMEs |
| Positive indigenisation lists | Ban import of listed items |

## Terms explained
- **Atmanirbhar Bharat** — "self-reliant India", the policy of building capability at home.
- **IDDM** — Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured.
- **Layered air defence** — several defensive systems (long-, medium-, short-range) covering each other.
- **Counter-drone system** — equipment to detect and destroy hostile drones.

## Don't confuse
The **S-400 'Sudarshan Chakra'** (an imported-then-inducted system) is different from **Mission Sudarshan Chakra**, the separate plan for a future *indigenous* air-defence shield.

## Remember it
"**Design at home, defend in layers**" — indigenise platforms, defend with stacked air-defence.

## TL;DR
- Indigenous platforms: Tejas LCA (HAL), Arjun MBT, INS Vikrant carrier.
- DAP 2020 prefers 'Buy (Indian-IDDM)'; iDEX funds start-ups; positive lists curb imports.
- Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025) followed the Pahalgam attack — precision strikes with layered air defence.
- It used integrated air defence: S-400 ('Sudarshan Chakra'), Akash SAM and counter-drone systems.
- Lesson: speed up indigenous air defence, drones and precision munitions.
keyPoints: Indigenous platforms: Tejas LCA (HAL), Arjun MBT, INS Vikrant carrier.
DAP 2020 prioritises 'Buy (Indian-IDDM)'; iDEX funds defence start-ups; positive indigenisation lists curb imports.

Mains angle: strategic autonomy vs imports, dual-use tech, and AP's stake via Sriharikota.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Space & Atmospheric Science Assets
items.body:
## In one line
The space and science facilities Andhra Pradesh hosts — above all India's only orbital spaceport at Sriharikota.

## The story
Andhra Pradesh is central to India's space effort because the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR)** sits on **Sriharikota**, a **barrier island** that separates the brackish **Pulicat Lake** from the Bay of Bengal. It is India's **primary (and only operational) orbital spaceport**. On **29 January 2025** the launch of **NVS-02** on a **GSLV-F15** rocket was the **100th launch from Sriharikota**; NVS-02 is a **second-generation NavIC** navigation satellite.

AP hosts other science assets too: **NARL (National Atmospheric Research Laboratory)** at **Gadanki, near Tirupati**, studies the atmosphere and space with its flagship **MST radar**; and the DRDO's **NSTL** at **Visakhapatnam** works on **underwater weapons**.

Private space is also taking root: **Skyroot's Vikram-S** (2022) was India's first private rocket (sub-orbital), and its orbital-class **Vikram-1** is planned to launch from Sriharikota (slated for 2026). **IN-SPACe** is the single-window autonomous body that authorises and promotes private space activity, and **NSIL** is ISRO's commercial arm.

## Why it matters
AP-specific space facts — Sriharikota's geography, the 100th-launch milestone, NARL Gadanki — are exactly the state-angle questions APPSC favours.

## Picture it

| Facility | Place | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| SDSC-SHAR | Sriharikota | Orbital launches (PSLV/GSLV/LVM3) |
| NARL | Gadanki (near Tirupati) | Atmospheric/space research; MST radar |
| NSTL (DRDO) | Visakhapatnam | Underwater weapons |

## Terms explained
- **Barrier island** — a long coastal island that shelters a lagoon (here, Pulicat Lake) from the sea.
- **MST radar** — Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere radar, for probing the atmosphere.
- **Second-generation NavIC** — newer, upgraded navigation satellites.
- **Sub-orbital vs orbital** — sub-orbital goes up and comes back; orbital circles the Earth.

## Don't confuse
The centre is named after **Satish Dhawan**, not Vikram Sarabhai. **SDSC-SHAR (Sriharikota)** does the **orbital launches**; **NARL (Gadanki)** does **atmospheric research** — different places, different jobs.

## Remember it
"**Sriharikota launches, Gadanki studies the sky**."

## TL;DR
- SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota (Pulicat barrier island) = India's primary orbital spaceport.
- NVS-02 (GSLV-F15, 29 Jan 2025) = 100th launch from Sriharikota; a 2nd-gen NavIC satellite.
- NARL, Gadanki (near Tirupati) does atmospheric/space research with its MST radar.
- Skyroot's Vikram-S (2022) was India's first private rocket; Vikram-1 is its orbital-class vehicle.
- IN-SPACe regulates/promotes private space; NSIL is ISRO's commercial arm.
keyPoints: SDSC-SHAR is on Sriharikota island (Pulicat Lake / Bay of Bengal) — India's primary orbital spaceport.
NVS-02 (GSLV-F15, 29 Jan 2025) was the 100th launch from Sriharikota; a 2nd-gen NavIC satellite.
NARL, Gadanki (near Tirupati) does atmospheric/space research with its MST radar.
Vikram-S (2022) was India's first private rocket; Vikram-1 is Skyroot's orbital-class vehicle.
IN-SPACe regulates/promotes private space; NSIL is ISRO's commercial arm.

items.title: Indian Space Programme — Milestones, Records & Recent Missions (to 2026)
items.body:
## From Thumba to the Moon's south pole

**In one line:** India's space story runs from a sounding rocket at Thumba (1963) to the first south-pole landing (2023), with a fixed list of "firsts" and records that examiners love.

**Why it is asked:** "India's first satellite", "first satellite on an Indian rocket", "SITE was for?", "104 satellites in one launch", "National Space Day" and the new launch sites are classic APPSC and UPSC items.

**The story**

The first rocket rose from **Thumba (TERLS), Kerala, on 21 November 1963** — a site chosen because it lies on the magnetic equator. India's first satellite, **Aryabhata (19 April 1975)**, flew on a Soviet rocket; **Rohini RS-1** became the first satellite put in orbit by an **Indian rocket, SLV-3, on 18 July 1980**, with Kalam as project director. **SITE (1975–76)** beamed educational TV to villages using NASA's ATS-6, and **EDUSAT (2004)** became the first satellite dedicated to education. Records followed: **PSLV-C37 carried 104 satellites in one launch (2017)**, and **Mangalyaan** reached Mars on the first attempt (2014). The day of Chandrayaan-3's landing, **23 August**, is now **National Space Day**.

### Firsts and records

| Milestone | Fact |
|---|---|
| **First rocket launch (Nike-Apache), 21 November 1963** | Thumba (TERLS), Kerala — on the magnetic equator |
| **India's first satellite** | Aryabhata — 19 April 1975, on a Soviet rocket |
| **First satellite placed in orbit by an Indian rocket** | Rohini RS-1 on SLV-3, 18 July 1980 |
| **APPLE (1981)** | India's first experimental communication satellite |
| **Bhaskara-I (1979)** | first experimental Earth-observation satellite |
| **SITE (1975–76)** | Satellite Instructional Television Experiment — educational TV to villages using NASA ATS-6 |
| **EDUSAT (GSAT-3, 2004)** | first Indian satellite built only for education |
| **AstroSat (2015)** | India's first multi-wavelength space observatory |
| **PSLV-C37 (15 February 2017)** | 104 satellites in a single launch — a world record at the time |
| **XPoSat (1 January 2024)** | India's first X-ray polarimetry satellite |
| **National Space Day** | 23 August — Chandrayaan-3 landing (2023) |

### Planetary and solar missions — details

| Mission | Key details |
|---|---|
| **Chandrayaan-1 (October 2008, PSLV-C11)** | confirmed water molecules on the Moon; carried the Moon Impact Probe |
| **Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)** | launched 5 November 2013 (PSLV-C25); entered Mars orbit 24 September 2014 — first Asian nation, first attempt |
| **Chandrayaan-2 (22 July 2019)** | orbiter still working; the Vikram lander crash-landed |
| **Chandrayaan-3 launch** | 14 July 2023 on LVM3-M4; landed 23 August 2023 near the south pole |
| **Aditya-L1 launch** | 2 September 2023 on PSLV-C57; seven payloads including the VELC coronagraph |
| **Chandrayaan-4 (approved September 2024)** | lunar sample-return mission |
| **Venus Orbiter Mission (approved September 2024)** | India's planned mission to orbit Venus |
| **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** | first module (BAS-1) targeted for 2028; full station by 2035 |
| **Gaganyaan astronaut-designates (named February 2024)** | Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla (all IAF) |

### Launch sites and recent launch events (2024–2025)

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Third Launch Pad at Sriharikota** | approved by the Union Cabinet in January 2025 (about ₹3,985 crore) for heavier next-generation rockets |
| **India's second spaceport (for SSLV)** | Kulasekarapattinam, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu (foundation stone February 2024) |
| **NVS-02 (January 2025)** | reached transfer orbit, but a valve fault stopped it from being raised to its planned orbit |
| **PSLV-C61 / EOS-09 (May 2025)** | failed because of a third-stage problem |
| **GSAT-N2 (GSAT-20), November 2024** | launched by SpaceX Falcon 9 because it was too heavy for Indian rockets |
| **CMS-03 (November 2025, LVM3-M5)** | heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil (about 4,400 kg) |

## Don't confuse
- **Aryabhata (1975)** was launched by the **USSR**; **Rohini (1980)** was the first on an **Indian rocket (SLV-3)**.
- **SITE (1975–76)** used an American satellite; **EDUSAT (2004)** was India's own education satellite.
- **Sriharikota (AP)** is the main spaceport and is getting a **third launch pad**; **Kulasekarapattinam (Tamil Nadu)** is the new **SSLV** spaceport.
- **National Space Day = 23 August**; National Science Day = 28 February; National Technology Day = 11 May.

**Remember it:** "Thumba '63, Aryabhata '75, Rohini '80, Mars '14, Moon south pole '23."

**TL;DR**
- First rocket from Thumba (1963); first satellite Aryabhata (1975); first on an Indian rocket Rohini/SLV-3 (1980).
- PSLV-C37 put up 104 satellites (2017); AstroSat (2015) and XPoSat (2024) are space observatories.
- Gaganyaan astronaut-designates: Nair, Krishnan, Pratap, Shukla; BAS-1 by 2028 and a full station by 2035.
keyPoints: First rocket launch (Nike-Apache), 21 November 1963 — Thumba (TERLS), Kerala — on the magnetic equator.
India's first satellite — Aryabhata — 19 April 1975, on a Soviet rocket.
Chandrayaan-1 (October 2008, PSLV-C11) — confirmed water molecules on the Moon; carried the Moon Impact Probe.
Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) — launched 5 November 2013 (PSLV-C25); entered Mars orbit 24 September 2014 — first Asian nation, first attempt.
Third Launch Pad at Sriharikota — approved by the Union Cabinet in January 2025 (about ₹3,985 crore) for heavier next-generation rockets.
India's second spaceport (for SSLV) — Kulasekarapattinam, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu (foundation stone February 2024).

items.title: ISRO Centres, Satellite Families & Orbits
items.body:
## Where ISRO builds, tests and runs its satellites

**In one line:** each ISRO centre has one job (rockets at Thiruvananthapuram, satellites at Bengaluru, engines at Mahendragiri, remote-sensing data at Hyderabad), and each satellite family serves one purpose from one kind of orbit.

**Why it is asked:** "URSC is located at?", "NRSC does what?", "GSAT-7 serves which force?", "GAGAN is for?" and "geostationary altitude" are common match and statement items.

**The story**

Rockets are designed at the **Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (Thiruvananthapuram)** and satellites at the **U R Rao Satellite Centre (Bengaluru)**. Liquid and cryogenic engines are tested at **IPRC Mahendragiri (Tamil Nadu)**. Satellite imagery is received and supplied by the **National Remote Sensing Centre (Hyderabad)**, and geostationary satellites are controlled from the **Master Control Facility at Hassan**. Communication satellites sit in **geostationary orbit about 35,786 km above the equator**, where one orbit takes 24 hours. Remote-sensing satellites fly much lower, in **polar sun-synchronous orbits** (about 500–900 km), crossing each place at the same local time.

### ISRO centres

| Centre | Location and role |
|---|---|
| **Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC)** | Thiruvananthapuram — designs launch vehicles |
| **U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC)** | Bengaluru — designs and builds satellites |
| **ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC)** | Mahendragiri, Tamil Nadu — tests liquid and cryogenic engines |
| **Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC)** | Valiamala (Thiruvananthapuram) and Bengaluru — liquid and cryogenic stages |
| **Space Applications Centre (SAC)** | Ahmedabad — satellite payloads and applications |
| **National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)** | Hyderabad — receives and supplies remote-sensing data |
| **Master Control Facility (MCF)** | Hassan (Karnataka) and Bhopal — controls geostationary satellites |
| **Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC)** | Bengaluru — runs the Gaganyaan programme |
| **ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC)** | Bengaluru — tracks satellites and launch vehicles |
| **Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST)** | Thiruvananthapuram — Asia's first space university (2007) |

### Satellites, orbits and their uses

| Satellite / orbit | Use or fact |
|---|---|
| **Geostationary orbit** | about 35,786 km above the equator; one orbit takes 24 hours — used by communication (INSAT/GSAT) satellites |
| **Polar sun-synchronous orbit** | about 500–900 km high — used by remote-sensing satellites, which pass each place at the same local time |
| **GSAT-7 ("Rukmini", 2013)** | Indian Navy's dedicated communication satellite |
| **GSAT-7A ("Angry Bird", 2018)** | Indian Air Force communication satellite |
| **Cartosat series** | high-resolution imaging for maps (cartography) |
| **RISAT series** | radar imaging — sees through clouds and at night |
| **Oceansat series** | ocean colour, sea winds and potential fishing zones |
| **Kalpana-1 (MetSat, 2002)** | India's first dedicated weather satellite |
| **INSAT-3DS (February 2024)** | meteorological satellite for weather forecasting and disaster warning |
| **Megha-Tropiques (2011) and SARAL (2013)** | joint missions with France (CNES) on tropical climate and ocean altimetry |
| **GAGAN** | GPS-aided GEO-augmented navigation for aviation — built by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India |
| **NavIC constellation** | seven satellites: three geostationary and four geosynchronous (inclined) |

## Don't confuse
- **VSSC (Thiruvananthapuram) = rockets; URSC (Bengaluru) = satellites; NRSC (Hyderabad) = remote-sensing data.**
- **Geostationary (about 35,786 km)** = communication and weather satellites; **sun-synchronous (low, polar)** = imaging satellites.
- **GSAT-7 = Navy; GSAT-7A = Air Force.** **GAGAN** supports aircraft navigation; **NavIC** is India's own regional navigation system.

**Remember it:** "Trivandrum launches, Bengaluru builds, Hyderabad sees, Hassan controls."

**TL;DR**
- VSSC Thiruvananthapuram, URSC Bengaluru, IPRC Mahendragiri, SAC Ahmedabad, NRSC Hyderabad, MCF Hassan.
- Geostationary orbit about 35,786 km (24-hour period); remote sensing from sun-synchronous orbits.
- Cartosat = maps; RISAT = radar; Kalpana-1 = first weather satellite; GAGAN = aviation navigation.
keyPoints: Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) — Thiruvananthapuram — designs launch vehicles.
U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) — Bengaluru — designs and builds satellites.
Geostationary orbit — about 35,786 km above the equator; one orbit takes 24 hours — used by communication (INSAT/GSAT) satellites.
GSAT-7 ("Rukmini", 2013) — Indian Navy's dedicated communication satellite.

items.title: Defence Technology — Missile Family, Platforms & Test Ranges
items.body:
## India's missiles, ships, aircraft and tanks

**In one line:** India now fields a full family of missiles (Agni, Prithvi, K-series, BrahMos, Astra, Akash) and indigenous platforms (INS Vikrant, INS Arihant, Tejas, Prachand, Pinaka), most tested off the Odisha coast.

**Why it is asked:** "range of Agni-V", "K-4 is launched from?", "first indigenous nuclear submarine", "BrahMos is named after?", "Astra is what type of missile?" and "where are missiles tested?" recur in UPSC and state PSC papers.

**The story**

The **Agni** series grew from Agni-I (about 700 km) to **Agni-V (over 5,000 km)**, which tested multiple warheads (MIRV) in **Mission Divyastra (2024)**. At sea, the **K-4 and K-15 (Sagarika)** missiles arm the **INS Arihant**, India's first home-built nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine (commissioned 2016), which gives India the sea leg of its **nuclear triad**. **BrahMos**, named after the **Brahmaputra and Moskva** rivers, was India's first major missile export (**Philippines, 2022 deal**). Most missiles are tested at the **Integrated Test Range, Chandipur** and **Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island (Wheeler Island)** in **Odisha**.

### Missiles

| Missile | Type / fact |
|---|---|
| **Agni series ranges** | Agni-I about 700 km; Agni-II 2,000+ km; Agni-III 3,000 km; Agni-IV 4,000 km; Agni-V 5,000+ km |
| **Agni-Prime (Agni-P)** | new-generation canister-launched ballistic missile (1,000–2,000 km) |
| **K-4 and K-15 (Sagarika)** | submarine-launched ballistic missiles fired from INS Arihant-class submarines |
| **Astra** | beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile (fired from Sukhoi and Tejas) |
| **BrahMos name** | from the Brahmaputra (India) and Moskva (Russia) rivers |
| **First major Indian missile export** | BrahMos to the Philippines (2022 deal; delivered from 2024) |
| **Nirbhay** | long-range subsonic cruise missile |
| **Pralay** | short-range quasi-ballistic surface-to-surface missile |
| **Rudram** | India's first indigenous anti-radiation missile (destroys enemy radars) |
| **MRSAM (Barak-8)** | medium-range surface-to-air missile developed with Israel |
| **Long-range hypersonic missile (November 2024)** | first flight test from Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island — range over 1,500 km |
| **Helina (Dhruvastra)** | helicopter-launched version of the Nag anti-tank missile |
| **Dhanush (missile)** | ship-launched naval version of Prithvi |

### Platforms and test ranges

| Platform / site | Fact |
|---|---|
| **INS Arihant** | India's first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine (SSBN), commissioned 2016 — completes the nuclear triad |
| **INS Arighaat (August 2024)** | India's second nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine |
| **INS Vikrant (commissioned 2 September 2022)** | India's first indigenous aircraft carrier, built at Cochin Shipyard |
| **Kalvari-class submarines (Project-75)** | Scorpene-design diesel-electric submarines built at Mazagon Dock with France |
| **Prachand (2022)** | HAL's indigenous Light Combat Helicopter, inducted in 2022 |
| **Pinaka** | DRDO multi-barrel rocket launcher system (also exported to Armenia) |
| **AMCA** | Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft — planned fifth-generation stealth fighter |
| **Rafale** | French fighter jets — 36 inducted into the IAF from 2020 |
| **MQ-9B (2024 deal)** | 31 armed drones bought from the USA |
| **Missile test sites** | Integrated Test Range, Chandipur and Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island (Wheeler Island) — both in Odisha |

## Don't confuse
- **INS Arihant** = nuclear **submarine** (SSBN); **INS Vikrant** = aircraft **carrier**; **Kalvari** = conventional (diesel-electric) submarines.
- **Astra** = air-to-air; **Akash** = surface-to-air; **Nag/Helina** = anti-tank; **Rudram** = anti-radiation; **Nirbhay** = subsonic cruise; **BrahMos** = supersonic cruise.
- **Missile tests happen in Odisha** (Chandipur, Kalam Island), not at Sriharikota, which is ISRO's spaceport in AP.

**Remember it:** "Agni goes up by a thousand: I-700, II-2,000, III-3,000, IV-4,000, V-5,000+."

**TL;DR**
- Agni-V (5,000+ km) tested MIRV in Mission Divyastra (2024); K-4/K-15 arm INS Arihant (2016), with INS Arighaat (2024) as the second SSBN.
- INS Vikrant (2022) is the first indigenous carrier; Prachand (2022) the Light Combat Helicopter; Pinaka the rocket launcher.
- BrahMos (Brahmaputra + Moskva) went to the Philippines; a long-range hypersonic missile was first tested in November 2024.
keyPoints: Agni series ranges — Agni-I about 700 km; Agni-II 2,000+ km; Agni-III 3,000 km; Agni-IV 4,000 km; Agni-V 5,000+ km.
K-4 and K-15 (Sagarika) — submarine-launched ballistic missiles fired from INS Arihant-class submarines.
INS Arihant — India's first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine (SSBN), commissioned 2016 — completes the nuclear triad.
INS Vikrant (commissioned 2 September 2022) — India's first indigenous aircraft carrier, built at Cochin Shipyard.

items.title: Defence Organisation, Labs, Policy & the Andhra Pradesh Angle
items.body:
## Who makes defence technology, where, and AP's part in it

**In one line:** DRDO's labs each specialise (missiles in Hyderabad, tanks at Avadi, underwater weapons at Visakhapatnam), policy pushes "Make in India", and Visakhapatnam is the Navy's eastern hub.

**Why it is asked:** "first CDS", "defence industrial corridors are in which states?", "NSTL is located at?", "Eastern Naval Command HQ" and "where was INS Arihant built?" are recurring APPSC and UPSC items.

**The story**

The post of **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)** was created in **December 2019**; **General Bipin Rawat** was the first. To cut imports, the government launched **iDEX (2018)** for defence start-ups and set up two **Defence Industrial Corridors — in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu**. Defence exports hit a record of about **₹23,622 crore in 2024–25**. Andhra Pradesh is central to the Navy: **Visakhapatnam** hosts the **Eastern Naval Command HQ**, the **Ship Building Centre** where the Arihant-class submarines were built, **Hindustan Shipyard Ltd** and DRDO's **NSTL**, while a new base, **INS Varsha at Rambilli**, is being built for nuclear submarines.

### DRDO labs and defence organisation

| Body / lab | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Defence Research and Development Laboratory (DRDL)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) — missiles (Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Missile Complex) |
| **Combat Vehicles R&D Establishment (CVRDE)** | Avadi, Chennai — tanks such as Arjun |
| **Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE)** | Bengaluru — drones (Rustom/TAPAS) |
| **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)** | post created December 2019; first CDS General Bipin Rawat |
| **iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence)** | launched 2018 — funds defence start-ups and MSMEs |
| **Defence Industrial Corridors** | two corridors — Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu |
| **Defence exports 2024–25** | record of about ₹23,622 crore |
| **SRIJAN portal (2020)** | lists imported defence items that Indian industry can make |

### Andhra Pradesh — defence and naval assets

| Asset | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Eastern Naval Command headquarters** | Visakhapatnam |
| **Ship Building Centre, Visakhapatnam** | where the Arihant-class nuclear submarines were built |
| **NSTL (DRDO)** | Visakhapatnam — torpedoes, mines and underwater weapon systems |
| **Hindustan Shipyard Ltd** | Visakhapatnam — shipbuilding PSU under the Ministry of Defence |
| **INS Varsha** | new naval base at Rambilli (Anakapalli district) for nuclear submarines |
| **Dolphin's Nose, Visakhapatnam** | headland that shelters the port and naval harbour |

## Don't confuse
- **DRDL (missiles)** is in **Hyderabad, Telangana**; **NSTL (underwater weapons)** is in **Visakhapatnam, AP**.
- **Defence corridors = Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu** (not AP).
- **Eastern Naval Command = Visakhapatnam**; Western = Mumbai; Southern = Kochi.

**Remember it:** "Vizag = ENC + Ship Building Centre + NSTL + HSL + INS Varsha (Rambilli)."

**TL;DR**
- First CDS: General Bipin Rawat (post created December 2019); iDEX 2018; corridors in UP and Tamil Nadu.
- Defence exports reached a record of about ₹23,622 crore in 2024–25.
- In AP, Visakhapatnam is the Navy's eastern hub; the Arihant-class submarines were built there.
keyPoints: Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) — post created December 2019; first CDS General Bipin Rawat.
iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) — launched 2018 — funds defence start-ups and MSMEs.
Eastern Naval Command headquarters — Visakhapatnam.
Ship Building Centre, Visakhapatnam — where the Arihant-class nuclear submarines were built.

items.title: For Mains — Space Technology & Defence
items.body:
## In one line
How to shape the ISRO/DRDO facts into a Mains answer for Paper-V (M5-3: Indian Space Programme — ISRO, satellites in health/education/weather; DRDO).

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Evolution / institutions | INCOSPAR 1962 → ISRO 1969 → DoS 1972; IN-SPACe, NSIL; DRDO 1958 |
| Achievements | Chandrayaan-3 (south pole), Aditya-L1, SpaDeX docking, NISAR; Agni-V MIRV, Mission Shakti |
| Societal applications | INSAT/GSAT (tele-education, telemedicine, broadcasting), IRS (resources, disaster), NavIC (navigation, agriculture) |
| Economic dimension | Space-sector reforms, start-ups (Skyroot, Agnikul), low-cost launches, growing space economy |
| Strategic dimension | Gaganyaan, indigenous NavIC, ASAT, nuclear triad; defence indigenisation (DAP 2020, iDEX) |
| Challenges / way forward | Funding scale, human-rating timelines, import dependence, dual-use ethics; scale R&D and private base |

## Data points to quote
- Chandrayaan-3 (23 Aug 2023); SpaDeX docking (16 Jan 2025, 4th nation); NISAR (30 Jul 2025, dual-band SAR).
- Agni-V MIRV under **Mission Divyastra (2024)**; **Mission Shakti (2019)** ASAT.
- Vision: **Bharatiya Antariksh Station 2035**, Indian on the Moon **2040**.
- Operation Sindoor (2025): value of integrated layered air defence.

## AP angle
**SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota** is India's primary spaceport (NVS-02 = 100th launch, Jan 2025); **NARL Gadanki** leads atmospheric research; AP can anchor a regional space-industry and defence-manufacturing ecosystem.

## Use in answers
- **Example:** cite Chandrayaan-3's south-pole landing and SpaDeX docking as proof of a self-reliant, rising space power.
- **Quote:** space as a tool "for the common man" (tele-education, telemedicine, disaster warning).
- **Diagram idea:** a satellite-applications wheel (comms · remote sensing · navigation · weather) around the citizen.

## TL;DR
- Structure: institutions → achievements → applications → economic/strategic → challenges → way forward, with an AP paragraph.
- Lead with Chandrayaan-3 and SpaDeX; always link satellites to citizen services.
- For defence: pair DRDO missiles with the indigenisation (DAP 2020/iDEX) and Operation Sindoor lesson.
keyPoints: Mains clause M5-3 (Paper-V): Indian Space Programme — ISRO, satellites in health/education/weather, DRDO.
Argue institutions → achievements → applications → economic/strategic → challenges → way forward.
Always connect satellites (INSAT/IRS/NavIC) to citizen services: tele-education, telemedicine, disaster warning.
Quote: Chandrayaan-3 (2023), SpaDeX docking (2025), Agni-V MIRV (2024), BAS 2035, Moon 2040.
AP angle: SDSC-SHAR Sriharikota (100th launch Jan 2025), NARL Gadanki, regional space/defence ecosystem.
